## Introduction

This tutorial introduces the structure and uses of the bash Terminal from within VS Code running on GitHub Codespaces. When most people use the word "terminal," they are referring to something like the bash Terminal, or some other shell which allows us to "talk" with the computer directly.

The older, more general term for the terminal is the "command line." All modern operating systems provide a command line, which sophisticated users can use to modify files and directories with commands like `pwd`, `ls`, `echo`, `mkdir`, `mv`, `rm`, and `cd`. This is the first of three Terminal tutorials. This one covers the core commands, paths, and redirection. Terminal 2 covers files and running programs. Terminal 3 covers wildcards, grep, and pipes.

Some material is from [*R for Data Science (2e)*](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/) by Hadley Wickham, Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel, and Garrett Grolemund.

###

You should be doing this tutorial in a repo named `terminal-1`. If you are not, create one and then connect to it. (Recall the rule: a tutorial's repo is named after its title, all in lower case, with spaces replaced by dashes --- "Terminal 1" becomes `terminal-1`.)

## Terminal

The lower section of the VS Code window is the "Panel," which is composed of a collection of "views," including Output, Problems, Ports, and Terminal. (Their labels appear in capitals --- **TERMINAL** --- across the top of the Panel.)

The Terminal view is, by far, the part of the Panel which we use most often. Within it you can run several *terminals* at once, each with its own tab on the right side of the Panel. A terminal is just a window for typing text to a program and reading the program's replies. The program is usually the bash **shell** --- a program whose whole job is to interpret your commands --- and that combination is what we call a bash Terminal. But a terminal can host other programs instead: an R Terminal is the same kind of window running R.

The icons on the right side of the Panel manage terminals: `+` opens a new bash Terminal (the drop-down arrow beside it offers other kinds, such as **R Terminal**), the split icon puts two terminals side by side, and the trash can closes the selected terminal. The first terminal's tab may carry a small warning triangle (⚠), which just means an extension activated after that terminal started. It is harmless.

![](images/terminal-on-open.png){width=90%}

This is a fresh Codespace, before any repo has been connected. The Panel holds one `bash` terminal showing the "YOUR CODESPACE IS READY" banner and, below it, the prompt: `codespace-starter $`. In your Codespace, now that you have connected to `terminal-1`, the prompt reads `terminal-1 $` instead.

### Exercise 1

Use the bash Terminal that is already open, or open a new one with the `+` icon. Hit the `Enter` key twice --- the string that reappears each time is the **prompt**, telling you bash is ready for your next command. Then run `pwd`. CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: terminal-1
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Use the bash Terminal that is already open, or open a new one with the + icon. Hit the Enter key twice -- the string that reappears each time is the prompt, telling you bash is ready for your next command. Then run pwd. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

Your answer should look something like:

```{.output}
terminal-1 $
terminal-1 $
terminal-1 $ pwd
/workspaces/terminal-1
terminal-1 $
```

The prompt is the name of the directory you are currently in --- `terminal-1` --- followed by a space and a dollar sign. The dollar sign marks the end of the prompt. You type commands after it. `pwd` prints the full path to that directory. (If you are working on your own computer rather than in a Codespace, your prompt will look different. Default prompts vary from computer to computer.) Every bash Terminal in a Codespace started from `codespace-starter` shows this short prompt, because `codespace-starter` set it up that way.

### Exercise 2

Let's **m**a**k**e a **dir**ectory called `example`. Run `mkdir example`. Run `ls` to confirm that the new directory exists inside the current working directory. CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: terminal-2
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Let's make a directory called example. Run mkdir example. Run ls to confirm that the new directory exists inside the current working directory. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

`mkdir` creates an empty directory. We --- and most other people --- use the terms "folder" and "directory" interchangeably.

### Exercise 3

Move into the `example` directory by running `cd example`. Run `pwd`. CP/CR.


```{r}
#| label: terminal-3
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Move into the example directory by running cd example. Run pwd. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

Your answer should look like:

```{.output}
terminal-1 $ mkdir example
terminal-1 $ ls
AGENTS.md  example
terminal-1 $ cd example
example $ pwd
/workspaces/terminal-1/example
example $
```

The `example` directory is one level below the directory in which you started. The other item `ls` listed, `AGENTS.md`, was placed in your repo by `connect-repo`.

### Exercise 4

Let's create a file called `my.txt`. Run `echo "" > my.txt`.

Run `ls` to confirm that the new file exists inside the current directory. CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: terminal-4
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Run ls to confirm that the new file exists inside the current directory. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
example $ echo "" > my.txt
example $ ls
my.txt
example $
```

`echo "" > my.txt` creates an empty file. `echo` just repeats whatever follows, which is an empty quote in this case. `>` redirects whatever comes before it into whatever comes after it.


### Exercise 5

Make a copy of `my.txt` called `my_2.txt` by using the `cp` command. That is, run `cp my.txt my_2.txt`. Confirm that this worked by running `ls`. CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: terminal-5
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Make a copy of my.txt called my_2.txt by using the cp command. That is, run cp my.txt my_2.txt. Confirm that this worked by running ls. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

Your answer should look like:

```{.output}
example $ cp my.txt my_2.txt
example $ ls
my_2.txt  my.txt
example $
```

`cp` takes two arguments: the file to copy and the name of the copy. The original is left untouched.

### Exercise 6

We rename files with the `mv` command, which is derived from **m**o**v**e. The first argument is the file we want to rename, and the second argument is the new name.

Rename `my.txt` to `fake.txt` by running `mv my.txt fake.txt`. Run `ls` to confirm. CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: terminal-6
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Rename my.txt to fake.txt by running mv my.txt fake.txt. Run ls to confirm. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

Your answer should look like:

```{.output}
example $ mv my.txt fake.txt
example $ ls
fake.txt  my_2.txt
example $
```

###

From the computer's point of view, **renaming** a file is the same thing as **moving** a file. In fact, moving is more general since it allows us to change both the name *and* the location of a file.

### Exercise 7

Let's **r**e**m**ove the file `fake.txt`. Run `rm fake.txt`. Run `ls` to confirm. CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: terminal-7
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Let's remove the file fake.txt. Run rm fake.txt. Run ls to confirm. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

Your answer should look like:

```{.output}
example $ rm fake.txt
example $ ls
my_2.txt
example $
```

Be careful with the `rm` command in the bash Terminal. Unlike moving files to Trash on your computer, it is (usually) irreversible.

### Exercise 8

We want to remove the `example` directory. But we can't do that while we are "located" in that directory. That is, the computer is aware that our Terminal process --- the entity that is executing our commands like `ls` and `cp` --- is currently working from the `example` directory.

Run `cd ..`. The "dot-dot" symbol --- `..` --- references the directory that contains the current directory. Run `pwd` to confirm. CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: terminal-8
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Run cd ... The \"dot-dot\" symbol -- .. -- references the directory that contains the current directory. Run pwd to confirm. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

Your answer should look like:

```{.output}
example $ cd ..
terminal-1 $ pwd
/workspaces/terminal-1
terminal-1 $
```

The prompt changed because we moved directories. The `..` symbol --- two periods --- always means the directory one level up, here the directory in which `example` is located.

### Exercise 9

Run `rm -r example` to remove the directory `example`. Then run `ls` to confirm. CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: terminal-9
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Run rm -r example to remove the directory example. Then run ls to confirm. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
terminal-1 $ rm -r example
terminal-1 $ ls
AGENTS.md
terminal-1 $
```

`-r` is an **option** that allows us to delete a directory. The `r` stands for **r**ecursive because, in order to delete a directory, you must also (recursively) delete every directory and file within that directory.

Don't leave junk files lying around.

## Paths

You will practice using paths both inside and outside the current working directory.

### Exercise 1

Every bash Terminal in this Codespace --- the one that was already open and any new one you open with `+` --- starts in `/workspaces/terminal-1`, your repo. VS Code normally starts a terminal in the folder you have open, and `connect-repo` also added a line to your shell's startup file that moves each new terminal into the repo, so you land there either way.

Run `pwd` to show your current working directory. CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: paths-1
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Run pwd to show your current working directory. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

The Activity Bar on the left side of VS Code includes several buttons. When you click one of these buttons, a view opens next to the Activity Bar. Pressing the button again closes that view.

The top button is the Explorer. Pressing it opens the Explorer pane, also called Project Explorer. This functions like the Mac Finder or the Windows Explorer.

Let's **c**hange the working **d**irectory to `paths`. Run `cd paths`. Run `pwd` to confirm that you have changed the working directory. CP/CR.


Your answer should look something like:

### Exercise 4

Use `mkdir` to make a directory called `lessons` inside `paths` by running `mkdir lessons`. Confirm that this worked by running `ls`. CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: paths-4
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Use mkdir to make a directory called lessons inside paths by running mkdir lessons. Confirm that this worked by running ls. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
paths $ mkdir lessons
paths $ ls
lessons
paths $
```

Because we changed working directories, the `lessons` directory is created inside the `paths` directory.

### Exercise 5

Make a directory within `lessons` called `fruits` by running `mkdir lessons/fruits`.

Run `ls lessons` to check to see if `fruits` exists inside the `lessons` directory. CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: paths-5
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Run ls lessons to check to see if fruits exists inside the lessons directory. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
paths $ mkdir lessons/fruits
paths $ ls lessons/
fruits
paths $
```

###

We could not, as before, simply give `fruits` as an argument to `mkdir` because then the directory would be created directly inside `paths`, the current working directory, rather than within `lessons`. To refer to a location other than the working directory, we need to use a **path**, which describes the location directory by directory. The path above is called a **relative path** because it uses the working directory as its starting point.

### Exercise 6

Let's change our working directory to `fruits`. Run `cd lessons/fruits`.

As you are typing this command, type only the `f` in `fruits` and then press the tab key (twice may be necessary on some computers). Pressing tab autocompletes the name of a file or directory.

CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: paths-6
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "As you are typing this command, type only the f in fruits and then press the tab key (twice may be necessary on some computers). Pressing tab autocompletes the name of a file or directory. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

Get in the habit of using the tab key. It saves typing and prevents misspelled file names.

### Exercise 7

Use `echo "" >` to make a text file inside `fruits`, named `pineapple.txt`. Recall that your current location --- i.e., your working directory --- is now `fruits`. So, to make a new file within `fruits`, you just need `echo "" > pineapple.txt`. Run `ls` to confirm. CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: paths-7
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Use echo \"\" > to make a text file inside fruits, named pineapple.txt. Recall that your current location -- i.e., your working directory -- is now fruits. So, to make a new file within fruits, you just need echo \"\" > pineapple.txt. Run ls to confirm. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
fruits $ echo "" > pineapple.txt
fruits $ ls
pineapple.txt
fruits $
```
###

`pineapple.txt` is still a relative path. Since the file is directly inside the working directory, the name of the file is all we need. `lessons/fruits/pineapple.txt`, which is what we would need if our working directory were `paths`, would produce an error. Those directories do not exist inside our actual starting point, `fruits`.

### Exercise 8

Use `echo` to make two more text files inside `fruits`, named `pear.txt` and `does-not-belong`. That is, run `echo "" > pear.txt && echo "" > does-not-belong`. Confirm by running `ls`. CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: paths-8
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Use echo to make two more text files inside fruits, named pear.txt and does-not-belong. That is, run echo \"\" > pear.txt && echo \"\" > does-not-belong. Confirm by running ls. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
fruits $ echo "" > pear.txt && echo "" > does-not-belong
fruits $ ls
does-not-belong  pear.txt  pineapple.txt
fruits $
```

`&&` joins two commands on one line: the shell runs the first, and then runs the second only if the first succeeded. (A single `&` means something quite different --- it sends the command before it to the background --- so be careful to type both ampersands.)

Let's change our working directory to `lessons`. Run `cd ..` to go to the folder immediately above the working directory. Use `pwd` to confirm that you are in the right directory. CP/CR.

### Exercise 10

Use `mkdir` to make a directory within `lessons`, named `tbd`. Run `ls` to confirm. CP/CR.


In the same way that `..` refers to the directory above the current directory, `.` --- a single period --- refers to the current directory.

### Exercise 11

Use `mv` to **m**o**v**e the file `does-not-belong` from the `fruits` directory to the `tbd` directory by running `mv fruits/does-not-belong tbd`. Run `ls tbd` to confirm.

CP/CR.

```{r}

#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Use mv to move the file does-not-belong from the fruits directory to the tbd directory by running mv fruits/does-not-belong tbd. Run ls tbd to confirm. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
lessons $ mv fruits/does-not-belong tbd
lessons $ ls tbd
does-not-belong
lessons $
```

###

We can act on files that are not in the working directory as long as we provide a path --- either relative, as here, or absolute --- to those files. Here neither `mv` nor `ls` acts on the current directory. Both act on directories below it, `fruits` and `tbd`.

### Exercise 12

Use `cd` to change the working directory up to `paths` by running `cd ..`. Confirm with `pwd`. Use `mv` and the `.` shorthand to move the directory `tbd` directly inside of `paths` by running `mv lessons/tbd .`. Confirm with `ls`. CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: paths-12
#| echo: false

  "Use cd to change the working directory up to paths by running cd ... Confirm with pwd. Use mv and the . shorthand to move the directory tbd directly inside of paths by running mv lessons/tbd .. Confirm with ls. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}

paths $ pwd
/workspaces/terminal-1/paths

```

When using `mv`, there is no difference between moving a directory and moving a file. `mv lessons/tbd .` moves the `tbd` directory, located inside `lessons`, to `.`, the current directory.

## Important symbols

We have seen two important symbols --- `..` and `.` --- already. This section will explore those along with `~`. The most common English terms for these symbols are "dot" for `.`, "dot dot" for `..`, and "tilde" for `~`. The `.` symbol indicates the current directory. The `..` symbol is for the directory one level above the current directory. The `~` symbol is for your "home" directory.

### Exercise 1

Use `mkdir symbols` to create a new directory called `symbols`. `cd` into that directory by running `cd symbols`. Confirm the change with `pwd`. Confirm that the directory is empty by running `ls`.

CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: important-symbols-1
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Use mkdir symbols to create a new directory called symbols. cd into that directory by running cd symbols. Confirm the change with pwd. Confirm that the directory is empty by running ls. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
terminal-1 $ mkdir symbols
terminal-1 $ cd symbols
symbols $ pwd
/workspaces/terminal-1/symbols
symbols $ ls
symbols $
```

Command-line commands are often called "shell" commands, because the bash shell is the program that reads and runs them.

### Exercise 2

But is the `symbols` directory really empty? Run `ls -a` to check. The `-` indicates an option to the `ls` command. The `a` option tells `ls` to return *a*ll the members of the directory.

CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: important-symbols-2
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "But is the symbols directory really empty? Run ls -a to check. The - indicates an option to the ls command. The a option tells ls to return *a*ll the members of the directory. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

Your answer should look like:

```{.output}
symbols $ ls -a
.       ..
symbols $
```

Every directory, even an "empty" one, includes `.` and `..`. The `.` is a link to the current directory, i.e., to the `symbols` directory in which we are currently located. The `..` is a link to the directory one level up, which is `/workspaces/terminal-1` in my case.

### Exercise 3

Run `ls ..` to examine the contents of the directory one level above the current directory. Then run `ls ../..` to look two levels up. CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: important-symbols-3
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Run ls .. to examine the contents of the directory one level above the current directory. Then run ls ../.. to look two levels up. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

My answer looks like this:

```{.output}
symbols $ ls ..
AGENTS.md  symbols
symbols $ ls ../..
codespace-starter  terminal-1
symbols $
```

###

One level up is your repo, where `symbols` sits beside `AGENTS.md`, the plain-text file `connect-repo` copies into every new repo. AI assistants such as Copilot read it from the repo root to learn the rules for working with you in this course. (The repo also contains hidden files, like the `.git` directory, but plain `ls` does not show those.) Two levels up is `/workspaces`, where your repo sits beside `codespace-starter`, the folder that supplied this Codespace, plus the repos from earlier tutorials if you have reused this Codespace. `..` means one level up, `../..` two, and so on.

### Exercise 4

Run `pwd` again. This returns the current working directory. Note that the return value is an **absolute path**. It tells you exactly where you --- meaning your Terminal session or instance --- are located on your computer. CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: important-symbols-4
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Run pwd again. This returns the current working directory. Note that the return value is an absolute path. It tells you exactly where you -- meaning your Terminal session or instance -- are located on your computer. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

My answer looks like this:

```{.output}
symbols $ pwd
/workspaces/terminal-1/symbols
symbols $
```

The absolute path for my current working directory breaks down into these components.

* The starting `/` indicates the root, or origin, of the file system. There is no directory higher than the root directory.

* `workspaces`, which is where GitHub Codespaces stores workspace folders.

* `terminal-1`, the repo in which you are doing this tutorial, followed by `symbols`, which is the directory we just created.

### Exercise 5

Run `cd` without any argument. Doing so changes your current directory to your home directory because that is the default behavior for `cd`. Run `pwd` to confirm where you are. CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: important-symbols-5
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Run cd without any argument. Doing so changes your current directory to your home directory because that is the default behavior for cd. Run pwd to confirm where you are. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

My answer looks like this:

```{.output}
symbols $ cd
~ $ pwd
/home/rstudio
~ $
```

In Codespaces, the home directory is usually `/home/rstudio`. After `cd`, the prompt reports `~` as the current working directory. `~` --- a tilde, pronounced "TIL-duh" --- is the symbol for the current user's home directory. The shorthands `.`, `..`, and `~` are not specific to any one command. They stand for paths and work anywhere a path does.

### Exercise 6

Use `cd`, along with the full path to the `symbols` directory that you determined above, to change the working directory back to the `symbols` directory. Run `pwd` to confirm. CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: important-symbols-6
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Use cd, along with the full path to the symbols directory that you determined above, to change the working directory back to the symbols directory. Run pwd to confirm. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
~ $ cd /workspaces/terminal-1/symbols
symbols $ pwd
/workspaces/terminal-1/symbols
symbols $
```

An absolute path works from anywhere, because it starts at the root of the file system rather than at the working directory.

### Exercise 7

Confirm that you are currently located in the `symbols` directory by running `pwd`. Run `cd ..` to move one directory up, out of the `symbols` directory. Delete the `symbols` directory with `rm -rf symbols`. CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: important-symbols-7
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Confirm that you are currently located in the symbols directory by running pwd. Run cd .. to move one directory up, out of the symbols directory. Delete the symbols directory with rm -rf symbols. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

Your answer should look like:

```{.output}
symbols $ pwd
/workspaces/terminal-1/symbols
symbols $ cd ..
terminal-1 $ rm -rf symbols
terminal-1 $
```

Note that `rm -rf symbols` and `rm -rf symbols/`, with the trailing slash, have the same effect. Except in unusual circumstances, including (or not including) the trailing slash in the name of a directory does not matter.

## Redirection

You have been creating files with `echo "" > my.txt` since the start of this tutorial. The `>` symbol **redirects** a program's output into a file. You should be back in your repo's top-level directory.

### Exercise 1

Run `echo`, giving it a quoted string with your first and last name as its argument. For me, that is `echo "David Kane"`. CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: redirection-1
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Run echo, giving it a quoted string with your first and last name as its argument. For me, that is echo \"David Kane\". CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

For me, this looks like:

```{.output}
terminal-1 $ echo "David Kane"
David Kane
terminal-1 $
```

`echo` just repeats its argument. By default, a program's output lands on your screen.

### Exercise 2

Now redirect that output into a file instead. Run `echo "Your First and Last Name Here" > me.txt` (with your actual name). Then run `cat me.txt`. `cat` prints a file's contents. CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: redirection-2
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Now redirect that output into a file instead. Run echo \"Your First and Last Name Here\" > me.txt (with your actual name). Then run cat me.txt. cat prints a file's contents. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
terminal-1 $ echo "David Kane" > me.txt
terminal-1 $ cat me.txt
David Kane
terminal-1 $
```

###

Nothing appeared on screen after the first command because `>` sent the output into `me.txt` instead. Be careful: `>` **overwrites** --- if `me.txt` had already existed, its old contents would be gone, with no warning.

### Exercise 3

To add to a file rather than overwrite it, use `>>`. Run `echo "I am learning bash." >> me.txt`, then `cat me.txt`, then clean up with `rm me.txt`. CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: redirection-3
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "To add to a file rather than overwrite it, use >>. Run echo \"I am learning bash.\" >> me.txt, then cat me.txt, then clean up with rm me.txt. CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{.output}
terminal-1 $ echo "I am learning bash." >> me.txt
terminal-1 $ cat me.txt
David Kane
I am learning bash.
terminal-1 $ rm me.txt
terminal-1 $
```

###

`>` overwrites. `>>` appends. Neither is limited to `echo`. Any command's output can be redirected, and AI agents build and extend files this way constantly. When you see `>` in a command an agent proposes, check what file it points at. Whatever is there now will be replaced.

## Summary

This tutorial introduced the structure and uses of the bash Terminal from within VS Code running on GitHub Codespaces.

The older, more general term for the terminal is the "command line." All modern operating systems provide a command line, which sophisticated users can use to modify files and directories with commands like `pwd`, `ls`, `echo`, `mkdir`, `mv`, `rm`, and `cd`. Some material is from [*R for Data Science (2e)*](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/) by Hadley Wickham, Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel, and Garrett Grolemund.

Learn more about the command line and related topics by reading [*The Unix Workbench*](https://seankross.com/the-unix-workbench/) by Sean Kross.
